why.correct: The coal power plant releases 6,000 of the 8,000 tons of SO2. Coal contains sulfur, and burning it turns that sulfur into SO2.
options: Cars and trucks lead for CO (18,000 tons) and NOx, but release just 60 tons of SO2.
Right: 6,000 tons, three quarters of the city total, because coal contains sulfur.
Factories release 1,500 tons of SO2, far less than the 6,000 tons from the coal plant.
Wood stoves lead for PM2.5 (650 tons), not SO2 (440 tons).

why.correct: Part over whole, times 100: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>200</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>tons</mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>tons</mtext></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{4{,}200\,\text{tons}}{8{,}000\,\text{tons}} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>52.5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 52.5\%</annotation></semantics></math>.

The coal plant made 6,000 of 8,000 tons of SO2, so SO2 falls by <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{6{,}000}{8{,}000} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>75</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 75\%</annotation></semantics></math>. NOx falls 30%, PM2.5 25%, and CO about 1%.
options: Right: the plant was 75% of the SO2, so closing it cuts SO2 by 75%.
The plant made 2,400 of 8,000 tons of NOx, a 30% cut. Vehicles make most NOx.
The plant made 400 of 1,600 tons of PM2.5, a 25% cut. Wood stoves make more.
The plant made 300 of 22,000 tons of CO, about 1%. Vehicles make almost all of it.

why.correct: Ozone near the ground is a secondary pollutant. Nothing emits it directly: it forms in the air when NOx and VOCs, both in the table, react in sunlight.
options: Smokestacks and tailpipes do not emit ozone; it forms later, in sunlit air.
The ozone layer is in the stratosphere, far above. The ozone we breathe forms near the ground.
Ozone (O3) and carbon monoxide (CO) are different gases with different sources.
Right: it is a secondary pollutant, made from two primary pollutants the table lists.

why.correct: Percent change is (new minus old) over old, times 100: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.05</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1.2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>1.2</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{(0.05 - 1.2)}{1.2} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>95.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= -95.8\%</annotation></semantics></math>, a fall of about 96%.
Under the Clean Air Act, the EPA phased lead out of gasoline. Car exhaust had been the main source of lead in city air, so the concentration fell as leaded fuel disappeared.
options: That cuts SO2 and mercury; most airborne lead came from gasoline in cars.
Trees do not remove lead from air on this scale; the source was removed.
Right: leaded gasoline was the main source, and the law phased it out.
The fall lasted 20 years and matches the fuel change, not the weather.

why.correct: Compare the drops: 1975 to 1980, 0.2; 1980 to 1985, 0.4; 1985 to 1990, 0.5; 1990 to 1995, 0.05 micrograms per cubic meter. The largest drop is 1985 to 1990.
options: That drop is 1.2 to 1.0, just 0.2.
Right: 0.6 to 0.1 is a drop of 0.5, the largest.
That drop is 1.0 to 0.6, or 0.4: large, but less than 0.5.
That drop is 0.1 to 0.05, the smallest in size.

why.correct: A primary pollutant leaves its source as it is. Carbon monoxide comes straight out of a tailpipe; the other three form later, in the air.
options: Right: it is emitted directly, so it is primary.
Ozone near the ground forms from NOx and VOCs in sunlight, so it is secondary.
The acid forms in the air from SO2 and water, so it is secondary.
The acid forms in the air from NO2, so it is secondary.

why.correct: Coal contains sulfur as an impurity. Burning it in power plants and industrial boilers turns the sulfur into SO2, the largest human source.
options: Gasoline is refined to be low in sulfur; cars are a major source of CO and NOx instead.
Wetland decomposition releases methane and CO2, not much SO2.
Drying paints and solvents release VOCs, not SO2.
Right: sulfur in the coal becomes SO2 when it burns.

why.correct: Air is about 78% nitrogen gas. At the high temperature inside an engine, nitrogen and oxygen from the air combine to form NO, which becomes NO2.
options: Nitrogen fixation is done by bacteria in soil and roots, not in fuel tanks.
Burning does not turn one element into another; sulfur becomes SO2.
Right: the nitrogen comes from the air drawn into the engine, not from the fuel.
Fertilizer is not added to fuel; the nitrogen comes from the air.

why.correct: Carbon monoxide from incomplete burning binds to hemoglobin in red blood cells more tightly than oxygen, so the blood carries less oxygen. It has no color or smell.
options: SO2 irritates airways but is not the brown gas; NO2 is brownish.
Right: CO binds hemoglobin and starves the body of oxygen.
CO2 traps heat; it does not thin the ozone layer, and it is not the dizzy-making gas here.
Gasoline sold today has no lead; the danger in a closed garage is CO.

why.correct: PM2.5 particles are 2.5 micrometers or smaller. They slip past the nose and throat into the deepest air sacs of the lungs, and some reach the blood.
options: Right: size decides how far a particle travels into the body.
Both are tiny solid or liquid particles; neither is a gas.
Both sizes have natural and human sources; the difference is size.
Particles do not turn into ozone; ozone forms from NOx and VOCs.

why.correct: A policy is a law or rule. The EPA standard that limits how much of a pollutant the air may contain is a rule; the others are devices or fuels.
options: A filter is a technology. A law requiring it would be the policy.
A bus is a technology. A rule or a tax would be the policy.
An engine design is a technology, not a law or rule.
Right: a legal limit is a policy, set under the Clean Air Act.

why.correct: The criteria pollutants are carbon monoxide, lead, nitrogen dioxide, ozone, particulate matter and sulfur dioxide.
options: CO2, methane and water vapor are not among the six criteria pollutants.
Mercury, ammonia and VOCs are not among the six criteria pollutants.
Right: these six have national air quality standards.
Nitrate and phosphate are water pollutants, not air pollutants.

why.correct: Let the units cancel: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>mi</mtext><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>g</mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>mi</mtext></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>kg</mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>g</mtext></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30{,}000\,\text{mi} \times \frac{4\,\text{g}}{1\,\text{mi}} \times \frac{1\,\text{kg}}{1{,}000\,\text{g}}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>120</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>kg</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 120\,\text{kg}</annotation></semantics></math> of NOx a year.
A policy is a rule with a target, and the answer says how the rule cuts the pollutant: plants switch to low-sulfur coal or clean their exhaust to stay under the limit.
The dashed ozone line peaks at 120 ppb at hour 14, which is 2 p.m., six hours after the NO peak.
options: That is the NO peak during the morning commute; ozone is still low then.
Right: the ozone line is highest at hour 14.
That is the NO2 peak. Ozone builds later, as sunlight strengthens.
At 6 p.m. ozone is falling; its peak came four hours earlier.

why.correct: Cars release mostly NO. In the air, NO reacts to form NO2, so NO2 builds up just after the NO from the morning rush.
options: Right: NO2 is made from the NO, so it peaks after it.
Engines release mostly NO all day; NO2 forms in the air.
Sunlight splits NO2 to help make ozone, not the other way round, and the NO2 peak is in the morning.
The NO2 rise follows the local NO rise from traffic, not a distant source.

why.correct: Sunlight splits NO2 into NO and a single oxygen atom. The oxygen atom joins an O2 molecule to make O3. So NO2 is used up as ozone is made.
options: The ozone layer stays far above; this ozone forms near the ground from NO2.
Wind does not explain why the two change in step with the sunlight.
The day is sunny; nothing in the graph points to rain.
Right: NO2 is used up as O3 is made, which is why one falls as the other rises.

why.correct: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>120</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>ppb</mtext><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>ppb</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>ppb</mtext></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{(120\,\text{ppb} - 10\,\text{ppb})}{10\,\text{ppb}} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 1{,}100\%</annotation></semantics></math>. Ozone was 12 times its 6 a.m. level.
Wednesday and Tuesday differ mostly in the sky: overcast Wednesday at 29 °C had 48 ppb, clear Tuesday at 31 °C had 96 ppb. Less sunlight, far less ozone.
options: Heat and sun both rise on Monday, so this alone cannot separate sunlight from temperature.
Thursday did not have the least ozone; overcast Wednesday did.
Right: similar temperatures, but the cloudy day made far less ozone.
Both days were clear, so this compares temperature, not sunlight.

why.correct: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>48</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>118</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>118</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{(48 - 118)}{118} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>59.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= -59.3\%</annotation></semantics></math>, a fall of about 59%.
Ozone forms fastest with strong sunlight and heat, so hot, clear afternoons, like Monday, bring the highest levels.
options: Little sunlight and cold air slow ozone formation.
Right: strong sunlight and heat make ozone fastest.
Without sunlight, ozone falls in the evening.
At night there is no sunlight to split NO2, so ozone is low.

why.correct: Nitrogen oxides from hot combustion and volatile organic compounds from fuel vapor and solvents react in sunlight to make ozone and other smog chemicals.
options: Right: NOx and VOCs plus sunlight make photochemical smog.
SO2 and soot make the gray, sooty kind of smog; CO2 is not a smog ingredient.
Neither is a key ingredient of photochemical smog.
Neither drives the sunlight reactions that make smog ozone.

why.correct: Without VOCs, NO reacts with ozone and breaks it back down. VOCs react with the NO instead, forming photochemical oxidants, so ozone is not used up and accumulates.
options: VOCs do not break into ozone; ozone forms from an oxygen atom freed from NO2.
VOCs do not cool the air; the effect is chemical.
VOCs are gases that do not block sunlight; smog forms in strong sun.
Right: the NO that would destroy ozone is tied up by VOC reactions.

why.correct: Sunlight is needed to split NO2 and make ozone. After dark no new ozone forms, and NO from evening traffic reacts with the ozone that is there, using it up.
options: Ozone near the ground does not drift up to the stratosphere overnight.
Ozone does not turn into SO2; they are different elements.
Right: no sunlight means no new ozone, and NO destroys the rest.
Trees do not absorb ozone through their roots.

why.correct: Same molecule, different place. High in the stratosphere O3 absorbs UV radiation; in the air we breathe it irritates and damages lung tissue and plant leaves.
options: Both are O3; only the location differs.
Right: location decides whether ozone helps or harms.
Ozone near the ground irritates lungs and harms crops.
Stratospheric ozone forms from O2 split by UV light, not from exhaust.

why.correct: Ozone irritates the airways and makes them swell, so people with asthma or other lung disease, children and people exercising hard outdoors are hurt most.
options: Right: active lungs take in more ozone, and asthma makes airways sensitive.
Indoor air in sealed, filtered buildings has much less ozone.
Smog builds in and downwind of the city, not far upwind.
Ozone peaks in the afternoon, and less is indoors.

why.correct: Photochemical smog needs sunlight to split NO2, and warmth speeds the reactions, so the same NOx and VOCs make more smog in sunny, warm city X.
options: Clouds cut the sunlight that smog needs; they do not add ozone.
Traffic supplies the NOx and VOCs, but sunlight is needed to react them.
Cool, cloudy weather slows ozone formation.
Right: sun and heat speed every step that makes ozone.

why.correct: Emission, then NO to NO2, then sunlight splitting NO2, then O + O2 forming O3, and VOCs keep the ozone from being destroyed.

<math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>72</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>96</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>96</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{(72 - 96)}{96} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= -25\%</annotation></semantics></math>: the rule went with a 25% fall in peak ozone.
Fewer car trips mean less NO and VOCs, the two ingredients sunlight turns into ozone. It fits a city and respects the "other than paints" limit.
In an inversion, temperature rises with height. At 6 a.m. it warms from -8 °C at the floor to 0 °C at 600 m, then cools again above that.
options: Above 600 m the air cools with height, which is the normal pattern.
Right: -8, -5, -1 and 0 °C rise with height, the reverse of normal.
The temperature rises only to 600 m; above that it falls again.
The air warms with height up to 600 m, which is an inversion.

why.correct: At 2 p.m. the temperature falls steadily with height (4, 2.5, 1, -0.5 ...). The sun has warmed the ground and the air above it, so the inversion has broken up.
options: Right: the warm ground heats the lowest air, which can rise again.
At 2 p.m. the ground is warmer (4 °C), not colder.
Between 600 and 1,000 m the 2 p.m. air also cools with height.
The lowest layers changed a lot: -8 to 4 °C at the floor.

why.correct: Subtract the lower reading from the higher: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mo>°</mo><mtext>C</mtext><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>8</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mo>°</mo><mtext>C</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mo>°</mo><mtext>C</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0\,°\text{C} - (-8\,°\text{C}) = 8\,°\text{C}</annotation></semantics></math> warmer at 600 m.

Smoke rises only while it is warmer and less dense than the air around it. At 600 m it meets the warm layer of the inversion, which is warmer than the rising smoke, so the smoke stops and spreads out under it.
options: The table shows temperature, not wind; the lid is the warm layer.
Air above 600 m is cooler again; the lid is the warm layer at 600 m.
Particles do not turn into gas; they collect under the warm layer.
Right: the inversion layer acts like a lid on the cooler air below.

why.correct: The morning peaks rise from 45 to 70 to 95 µg per m³: each day adds to particles that the inversion kept from clearing.
options: Read the graph left to right: the peaks rise with time.
Only the first peak is 45; the next two are higher.
Right: the peaks climb by about 25 each day.
PM2.5 is lowest each afternoon and peaks in the morning.

why.correct: By afternoon the sun has warmed the ground, the inversion breaks, and the warmed air rises and mixes, carrying particles up and away. At night the inversion forms again.
options: Some heating continues; the daily rhythm follows the inversion.
Right: rising air carries the particles up and out of the valley.
Particles are not destroyed by sunlight this way; they are mixed away.
Afternoon air near the ground is warmer and rises, not sinks.

why.correct: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>95</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>45</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>45</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{(95 - 45)}{45} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>111.1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 111.1\%</annotation></semantics></math>, so the peak more than doubled.
The particles come from the valley's own sources and are trapped there, so cutting those sources while the inversion lasts works best. A no-burn day for wood stoves does that.
options: Right: it cuts a main source of the particles that are being trapped.
Smoke would still stop under the warm layer, and homes are not the only fix.
Grass may cut dust slightly but not the smoke and exhaust that build up.
Open windows let the polluted outdoor air in.

why.correct: Normally the air is warmest near the ground, which the sun heats, and it gets cooler with height. Warm air near the ground can rise and carry pollutants up.
options: That is the pattern of an inversion, not the normal one.
Temperature changes with height in the lowest layer.
Normally it cools with height; an inversion reverses that.
Right: that is the normal pattern, which lets warm air rise.

why.correct: A layer of warm air sits on top of cooler, denser air. The cool air cannot rise through the warmer, lighter air above it, so it and its pollutants stay near the ground.
options: In an inversion the air near the ground is the cool air, not the warm air.
An inversion changes how air moves, not what the pollutants are.
Right: the warm layer acts as a lid on the cool air below.
The pollutants are trapped because the air cannot rise, not because they sink.

why.correct: On clear, calm nights the ground loses heat fast and cools the air touching it. In a valley the cold air pools under warmer air, and with no wind nothing mixes it.
options: Wind mixes the air, and clouds keep the ground from cooling fast.
Right: the ground cools fast and cold air pools in the valley.
The sun-warmed ground and storm winds mix the air.
Rain and wind keep the air stirred, which breaks layers up.

why.correct: The town's smoke and gases kept being added to the same shallow layer of air, so their concentration rose day after day and irritated people's lungs.
options: Right: same sources, no escape, so the levels climbed.
Cold air alone does not explain the steady rise over five days.
The sources stayed about the same; the air stopped clearing.
The ozone layer stays in the stratosphere; the cause was trapped emissions.

why.correct: Both sit in basins ringed by mountains, where inversions are common. The mountains block wind on the sides, and the warm layer acts as a lid on top.
options: Both are at fairly low latitudes, with plenty of sun.
Both have heavy traffic, a main source of their smog.
Neither is especially rainy; rain would help clean the air.
Right: mountains on the sides plus an inversion lid trap the air.

why.correct: The town cannot stop the inversion, so the fix must cut emissions while the lid is on. A rule tied to inversion forecasts does exactly that.
The sun warms the ground, which warms the lowest air until it is warmer than the layer above and can rise, or a weather front brings wind that mixes the layers.
options: A clear, calm night strengthens an inversion; it does not end it.
Smoke cannot rise through the warm layer, so it cannot push it.
Right: either one lets the lowest air rise and mix again.
Snow reflects sunlight, keeping the ground cold, which can make inversions last.

why.correct: Cooling is the rate times the height: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mo>°</mo><mtext>C</mtext><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>6.5</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mo>°</mo><mtext>C</mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>m</mtext></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>m</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\,°\text{C} - \frac{6.5\,°\text{C}}{1{,}000\,\text{m}} \times 1{,}000\,\text{m}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2.5</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mo>°</mo><mtext>C</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= -2.5\,°\text{C}</annotation></semantics></math>. The table shows -3.5 °C, a little colder than expected.
As PM2.5 rises, visibility falls, and as PM2.5 clears, visibility returns: an inverse relationship. Particles scatter and absorb light, which makes haze.
options: On day 5, PM2.5 is highest and visibility is lowest, so they move oppositely.
Right: the two lines move in opposite directions, an inverse relationship.
The two change on the same days, not two days apart.
They move in step, in opposite directions, across all ten days.

why.correct: Particles scatter and absorb sunlight, so less light travels straight from distant objects to your eye, and the air looks hazy.
options: Right: that is what haze is.
Particles are tiny solids or droplets; they scatter light in many directions.
The haze comes from the particles themselves, not from rain clouds.
Particles do not remove oxygen; they block and scatter light.

why.correct: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>km</mtext><mo>−</mo><mn>40</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>km</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>40</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>km</mtext></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{(2\,\text{km} - 40\,\text{km})}{40\,\text{km}} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= -95\%</annotation></semantics></math>, a 95% fall. Visibility fell, so the percent change is negative.
PM2.5 reached 110 to 150 µg per m³ on those days. Particles that small reach deep into the lungs and the blood, so less time outdoors means less exposure.
options: Low visibility matters for driving, but the health advice is about breathing particles.
Smoke does not raise stratospheric ozone; the risk here is particles.
Outdoor CO2 from a distant fire does not get high enough to replace oxygen.
Right: the advice targets the days of highest exposure.

why.correct: Natural sources: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>180</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>240</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">180 + 60 = 240</annotation></semantics></math> thousand metric tons. Total: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>180</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>90</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">180 + 60 + 90 + 50 + 20</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>400</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 400</annotation></semantics></math>. Share: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>240</mn><mn>400</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{240}{400} \times 100 = 60\%</annotation></semantics></math>.
Unpaved roads and construction give 90 thousand metric tons a year, the largest human source. Paving roads and wetting construction sites target it.
options: Lake bed dust is the largest source overall, but it is natural, not human.
At 20 thousand metric tons, it is the smallest human source here.
Right: at 90 thousand metric tons it is the largest human source.
Plowed fields give 50 thousand metric tons, less than roads and construction.

why.correct: Dry lake beds are the largest source. More exposed, dry sediment means more dust lifted by wind, so PM10 would rise even with no change in human activity.
options: Evaporation does not make PM10; exposed dry sediment does.
Right: the largest source would grow.
Natural changes still change emissions; dust would increase.
The table gives no reason to expect fewer people; the dust source grows.

why.correct: Volcanoes release CO2 from deep in the Earth. Respiration, decomposition and wildfires are other natural sources.
options: Right: volcanoes release CO2, sulfur dioxide and ash.
Burning gasoline releases CO2, but it is a human source.
Cement making releases CO2, but it is a human activity.
Photosynthesis takes CO2 out of the air; it is not a source.

why.correct: Volcanic ash, sea salt spray, pollen and desert dust are natural; diesel exhaust, coal burning and construction dust are human.
options: The order is reversed: diesel is human and volcanic ash is natural.
Both of these are human sources.
Both of these are natural sources.
Right: sea spray is natural, diesel soot is human.

why.correct: Decomposers break down dead matter and release the carbon as CO2 through cellular respiration.
options: Photosynthesis takes CO2 in; it does not release it.
Sedimentation buries carbon in rock over long times; it does not release CO2 from leaves.
Right: decomposers respire, releasing CO2.
Condensation is water vapor turning to liquid; it releases no CO2.

why.correct: Human burning of fossil fuels and cement making release roughly 100 times more CO2 each year than all the world's volcanoes combined (USGS estimates).
options: This common claim is wrong; human emissions are much larger.
Right: estimates put human emissions at about 100 times volcanic emissions.
They are not close; human emissions are about 100 times larger.
Volcanoes add CO2; they do not remove it.

why.correct: Particles hurt the lungs whatever their source. Smoke from lightning-started wildfires and desert dust storms raise PM2.5 and hospital visits.
options: Right: natural smoke particles harm lungs just as human smoke does.

why.correct: Radon and its decay products give off radiation inside the lungs when breathed in. Over years this damages lung cells, and radon is a leading cause of lung cancer after smoking.

why.correct: CO has no color or smell, so a detector that sounds an alarm is the key safeguard, along with yearly furnace inspections and vents that work.
options: Radon kits measure radon, not carbon monoxide.
Fresheners add VOCs and do not remove CO, which has no odor anyway.
